p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for four and a half months, and AR 2207, the report on the departure stage's main valve, is open again, since he reopened it in February.
In April a spring blizzard hit the stand during the valve campaign, and Sam got the night crew through it.

The campaign caught one real repeat of the 2059 fault, 31 milliseconds on the third close after a chilldown, and Nell Garrity of Aldergrove, the valve's maker in Pueblo, brought her company's records from the Petrel's valve.
Sam funded a $6.4 million second test article to find out why the valve does it.
Now the readiness board has called Wendell, without company management, to its May 26 session, with Ruth Calder writing the record.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Calvin Osterhout. The ARA's comptroller, who answers for the partners' money.

Thursday, May 26, 2061. 8:40 AM. The hallway outside Room 4 in the federal building downtown had one wooden bench in it, and Sam sat on the bench with his jacket across his knees and didn't go in. The docket notice had said company management attendance was not required. He'd read that the way he'd read a caution in a tech order, which was as an instruction with a reason behind it he didn't have to be told.

Wendell went in at 8:55 with the shoebox of notebooks under one arm, the rubber bands on, and a canvas bag over his shoulder with a second set in it. Sam's text the week before had said to bring two sets. Wendell had texted back one word, and the word had been Copies.

The door had a small window with wire in the glass. Through it Sam could see the end of a long table, a pitcher of water, and a hand with a green pen in it, writing. He looked at the floor after that. It was a good floor, old terrazzo with brass strips in it, and he learned it well over the next three hours.
At 12:05 the door opened and Wendell came out and set the shoebox on the bench and sat down beside it. He looked tired in the way men his age look after they've talked more than they meant to.
She asked me the right question. He took the rubber band off one bundle and put it back on. Whether anybody asked me, in fifty nine, if the valve had noise. Or only the stand.

Nobody did. He looked down the hallway. She didn't say anything to me about it. She said it to the record. She read it back in that voice and had the clerk write it down. That's how she does it now, I guess. A pause. She asked if she could hold one of the notebooks. The one from thirty four. I said they're mine, I want them back. She laughed. He seemed to think about that. Haven't heard her laugh since 2035.
The minutes came through the docket system on Friday at 1:12 PM, in the board's capitals, the way everything from the board came.

INDEPENDENT READINESS BOARD QUESTION 61-07 SESSION OF THURSDAY, MAY 26, 2061 MINUTES (EXTRACT). MEMBER CALDER DISCLOSED PRIOR SERVICE WITH THE TEST CONDUCTOR (PETREL, 2034 TO 2035). THE CHAIR RULED NO CONFLICT. 1. AR 2207 (HALCYON DEPARTURE STAGE MOIV-1) IS OPEN AT CRITICALITY 1. FLIGHT RULE 2.36 APPLIES IN FULL. 2. THE BOARD RECEIVED THE ORIGINAL STAND RECORDS OF 2059 AND 2061 FROM THE TEST CONDUCTOR OF RECORD. 3. THE BOARD WILL REVIEW THE PROGRAM'S PLAN FOR REPRODUCTION AND LIFE TESTING AT ITS AUGUST SESSION. 4. THE BOARD REQUESTS THAT THE COST AND SCHEDULE OF THE AR 2207 INVESTIGATION BE SHOWN AS A SEPARATE LINE IN THE PROGRAM'S SUBMISSIONS TO THE ARA PARTNER FINANCE COMMITTEE, SO THAT IT IS VISIBLE TO THE PARTNERS AND CANNOT BE ABSORBED. RAPPORTEUR: R. CALDER. APPROVED: THE CHAIR.
He read item four three times. Cannot be absorbed. It was a strange thing for a safety board to care about, and then, on the third time, it wasn't strange at all.

On Wednesday, June 1, a letter came from the ARA comptroller's office, signed by Calvin Osterhout in the blue ink of a man who signed a lot of letters. The ARA Partner Finance Committee would hold its annual review of the Halcyon program on Thursday, July 14, in Washington. Status date June 30. The program would present cost and schedule performance, its estimate at completion, and the state of its reserves. The meeting would be in the ballroom of a hotel near Union Station, the letter said, because the ARA's own building didn't have a room that held eleven delegations and their advisers. Sam put the date in his phone and in the program calendar, and he wrote WASHINGTON on the whiteboard behind his desk with the date under it, and then he went back to work.
Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 627.

June was numbers. Quinn asked every control account owner for a bottom up estimate of what was left, due July 8, and got eleven polite emails asking what a control account was. The man from finance who'd carried the 2058 bid into the big room in March came back and stayed. Sam's logs to Ada that month were about tomatoes and the weather on the stand, and he recorded them at the kitchen table with Quinn's spreadsheet open on the laptop beside the tablet, out of the frame. He was fairly sure it was out of the frame.
Ruth's Console Log, page five: point nine.

Ruth's console log, 181 days before launch. oh seven hundred, agency budget review, hq, 9TH floor. coffee worse than the numbers. oh seven thirty, numbers. CPI 0.87. SPI 0.84. oh seven forty five, stand second shift since july paid from management reserve. no change request. everybody knew. nobody wrote it down. writing it down now. oh eight hundred, reserve left: 11 percent of what we started with. oh eight thirty, administrator: can I say ninety. I said call it 0.9. he said 0.9 and improving. I didn't say improving. I didn't say not. oh nine hundred, slide 6: reserve adequate. my initials on it. eleven hundred, oversight staffer asks what adequate means. administrator answers. I let him. fourteen hundred, did the arithmetic on the plane. the rounding is 46.4 million. a shelf valve on a stand was 3. seventeen thirty, L minus 181. wrote this in the air so i'd have to.
I've told you twice now that I'm not your mentor, and here's a page that proves it. Nobody should learn this from me. I'll teach it to you anyway, because I'm the one who has the page.

Point eight seven. Read it out loud and it sounds like point nine. That's the whole trick, and it's why it works. Nobody in the room that morning thought I'd lied, including me. The Administrator wanted a number he could say, I gave him one that was closer to the truth than most numbers said in that building, and the staffer who asked what adequate meant got an answer from a man who believed it. Then on the plane I divided the budget by both numbers, because that's what an engineer does when she can't sleep, and the difference between them was forty six point four million dollars. I'd rounded away fifteen life tests on a shelf valve. You've read page four. You know which one we didn't run.

This page is R6, plan and manage finance, and R9, evaluate project status, and under both of them a value the Code calls honesty. Its description is short enough to memorize: honesty is our duty to understand the truth and act in a truthful manner both in our communications and in our conduct. I'd like you to notice that the first half is understanding. You can't report a number truthfully if you haven't done the arithmetic on it. I hadn't, at 0830. I did it at 1400, which is the wrong order.

How the exam asks it. When a scenario offers you a way to make a number look better without changing the work, the answer is to report the accurate figure with its cause and a plan. Rounding up, reframing, and footnoting are the distractors.

Start with the words, because the exam uses them precisely. The cost estimate is what the work packages are expected to cost, added up. Add the contingency reserve, the money for identified risks, and you have the cost baseline: approved, time phased, and the thing you measure against. Add the management reserve, the money for things nobody identified, and you have the project budget. Contingency is inside the baseline and the project manager manages it. Management reserve is outside it, controlled by management or the sponsor, and released through change control, which changes the baseline when it's used.

You saw it on page four's numbers in small. The test article's estimate was $6.4 million. Its risks added up to $800,000 of contingency, so its cost baseline was $7.2 million. The ARA held $500,000 of management reserve over it, so the budget was $7.7 million. The same arithmetic works for a ship. Halcyon's cost baseline is $2,400 million, contingency included. The ARA holds $72 million of management reserve over it. The budget is $2,472 million.

When an identified risk happens, its response is paid from contingency. Moving contingency into a work package doesn't change the cost baseline by a dollar, because the money was already in it; it changes where the money sits, and you report the draw and what's left so nobody thinks the reserve is bigger than it is. Management reserve is for the unforeseen. It isn't for an overrun. When the work costs more than you planned, the answer is a new estimate and a decision about funding or scope, made in the open, not a quiet withdrawal from the drawer.

Then there's the money you can actually spend in a given year, which is not the same as the money you're allowed to spend in total. Governments fund by fiscal year. The funding requirements come in chunks, a staircase over the smooth curve of the baseline. Funding limit reconciliation compares the planned spending in each period with the funding limit for that period and, when the plan spends more than the limit, moves work. Say a program plans to spend $780 million in a fiscal year and its funders have capped it at $720 million. Sixty million dollars of work has to move into the next year, and you move it where there's float first, so the end date holds. If there isn't enough float, the schedule changes, and you say so. Reconciling to the funding limit can revise the schedule and the resource plan. It can't make the money appear.

How the exam asks it. Baseline estimates contingency. Budget baseline management reserve. A spending peak above a funding limit is solved by funding limit reconciliation, moving work within float first. Using management reserve to cover an overrun is a trap.

Earned value rests on three numbers measured at a status date. Planned value, PV, is the budgeted cost of the work you planned to have done by now. Earned value, EV, is the budgeted cost of the work you actually got done. Actual cost, AC, is what you actually spent doing it. All three are cumulative, all three are in money, and two of them are easy. PV comes from the baseline. AC comes from the books. EV is where people lie, usually without meaning to.

EV has to come from rules agreed before the work starts. The simplest is zero one hundred: no credit until the work package is finished. There's fifty fifty: half the credit when it starts, half when it's done. For long packages there are weighted milestones, a share of the budget earned at each objective, checkable event. Percent complete is a legitimate rule too, when it's measured against something physical you can count, not estimated. What EV must never come from is a person's sense of how far along they are. Ninety percent complete is the most popular number in engineering, and it stays ninety percent for months.

Two traps you'll meet. Using percent spent as percent complete makes EV equal AC, so cost performance is always perfect and always wrong. And money committed isn't money spent: a purchase order for a test article in June is a commitment, and it becomes actual cost when the work is done and invoiced, not before.

Agile work earns value too, and the exam expects you to know how. The release plan has a budget and a number of story points. Earned value is the share of points accepted against the definition of done, times the budget for the release. If a release is 400 points for $8 million and the team has accepted 160, the release has earned $3.2 million, whatever was spent getting there and however much is almost done. Almost done earns nothing in a sprint, which is the best rule agile ever gave the rest of us.

How the exam asks it. If a question gives "percent complete" and the budget at completion, EV percent complete x BAC. For agile, EV (accepted points planned points) x release budget. Never claim EV for work that is started but not finished unless the earning rule says so.

Every earned value formula starts with EV, and that's the only thing you need to memorize about the order. Schedule variance is EV minus PV. Cost variance is EV minus AC. Negative is bad for both. The schedule performance index is EV divided by PV. The cost performance index is EV divided by AC. Below 1 is bad for both.

Halcyon's numbers on June 30, in millions: PV 1,250, EV 1,200, AC 1,280. Schedule variance: 1,200 minus 1,250, minus 50. Cost variance: 1,200 minus 1,280, minus 80. SPI: 1,200 divided by 1,250, 0.96. CPI: 1,200 divided by 1,280, 0.9375, which you'll write as 0.94. For every dollar the program has spent, it has earned ninety four cents of planned work. For every dollar of work it planned to have done, it has done ninety six cents.

Two things about SPI the exam likes. It's measured in money, so it tells you how much planned work is done, not whether the critical path is on time; a program can have a fine SPI with the one activity that matters late. Check it against the network. And at the end of every project SPI goes back to 1.0, because eventually all the planned value is earned, late or not. Read it with the dates beside it.

And one thing about CPI that matters more than any formula. It tends to settle early. Once a big program is a fifth of the way through, its CPI rarely recovers much, because the habits and prices that made it are still there. Hope is not a trend line.
How the exam asks it. EV first, always. SV EV minus PV, CV EV minus AC, SPI EV PV, CPI EV AC. Under zero or under one is bad.

The estimate at completion, EAC, is what you now expect the whole project to cost. The estimate to complete, ETC, is what's left to spend, so EAC is AC plus ETC. The variance at completion, VAC, is BAC minus EAC, and negative means you'll finish over. There are four common ways to get the EAC, and the exam's real question is always which one fits the situation. Here they are with Halcyon's numbers and a BAC of 2,400.

If the variance so far is typical and will continue, EAC BAC divided by CPI. 2,400 divided by 0.9375 is 2,560, so ETC is 1,280 and VAC is minus 160. If the variance so far was a one time event that won't recur, and the rest will go at the budgeted rate, EAC AC (BAC minus EV). 1,280 1,200 is 2,480, VAC minus 80. If the original estimate was fundamentally wrong, you throw the formulas away for the remaining work and re-estimate it from the bottom up: EAC AC bottom up ETC. Halcyon's control account owners said 1,320, so 2,600, VAC minus 200. And if both cost and schedule performance will drive what's left, because a fixed date will make you buy back time, EAC AC (BAC minus EV) divided by (CPI times SPI). 0.9375 times 0.96 is 0.90, so 1,280 1,200 divided by 0.90, which is 1,280 1,333.3, or 2,613.3, VAC minus 213.3.

Four numbers between 2,480 and 2,613, from one set of facts. Every one of them is arithmetic. Only one of them is true for a given program, and the choice is a statement about why the program is over: a storm that passed, a habit that's staying, an estimate that was wrong, or a date that won't move. Choose the formula from the cause, write down why, and check it against a bottom up estimate when you can. If the formula you chose happens to be the lowest of the four, and the cause doesn't support it, that's not a forecast. That's page five.

How the exam asks it. Read the cause. "Expected to continue": BAC CPI. "One time" or "won't recur": AC (BAC minus EV). "Original estimate flawed": AC new ETC. "Must meet the date" with poor cost and schedule: the CPI x SPI formula.

The to complete performance index, TCPI, turns the question around. It asks how efficient the rest of the work would have to be to land on a target. It's the work remaining divided by the money remaining. Against the original budget: TCPI (BAC minus EV) divided by (BAC minus AC). Against an approved new estimate: (BAC minus EV) divided by (EAC minus AC).

Halcyon, against its BAC: 2,400 minus 1,200 is 1,200 of work left. 2,400 minus 1,280 is 1,120 of money left. 1,200 divided by 1,120 is 1.07. The program has been running at 0.94. To finish on the original budget it would have to run at 1.07 for the rest of its life, which is about fourteen percent better than it has run so far. You can say that's a stretch goal. You'd be saying it to people who'll remember.

Against an EAC of 2,600: 1,200 divided by 2,600 minus 1,280, which is 1,200 over 1,320, or 0.91. That one needs the program to keep doing roughly what it's been doing. A TCPI near the current CPI is a forecast. A TCPI well above it is a wish, and the honest thing to do with a wish is to say it out loud as one, and then bring the people who decide a choice: more money, less scope, more time, or some of each.

The rule I wish I'd been handed: never let anybody force the estimate to complete so the EAC comes out equal to the BAC. Working the numbers backward from the answer you want is the oldest move in the building.

How the exam asks it. TCPI above 1 means the rest must be done more efficiently than budgeted. Compare it with the CPI to date; a large gap means the target isn't credible and needs a decision, not a pep talk.

B3, manage and control changes. Execute the change control process, communicate the status of proposed changes, implement approved changes, update the documentation. Sooner or later a sponsor will ask you to rebaseline, and sometimes she'll be right. A baseline should change when an approved change has changed the work: new scope, a funded response to a risk, a new date the funders agreed to. That goes through change control, the approved change gets folded in, and the documents say when and why.

A baseline should not change to make the variances go away. If you reset PV, EV, and AC to today and start the indexes at 1.00, you haven't fixed the program. You've removed the instrument. The history of how you got here is the most useful data you have about how you'll do from here. Keep it, report it beside the new baseline, and let the people reading it see both.

The same goes for the reserves. When any reserve is drawn, say how much and what's left. Ours was management reserve, drawn for a second shift on the stand without a change request, because it was quicker, and by December eleven percent of it was left and the slide said adequate. Reserve that's been spent and not reported is still spent. It's just spent in the dark.

How the exam asks it. A rebaseline follows an approved change. If the only purpose is to make variances disappear, it's the wrong answer. A sponsor approving a baseline change outside the change process is also wrong.

P8 asks you to understand reporting requirements and create reports aligned with sponsors and stakeholder expectations. Aligned with what they need to decide, I'd add, which isn't the same as aligned with what they'd like to hear. An oversight body needs a few things on one page: the indexes, the forecast with its range, why it's what it is, what you're doing about it, and the decisions you need from them. It doesn't need sixty slides. It doesn't need a trend line with the axis cut so a dip looks like a hill.

B1 is governance: the rules, the reporting, the escalation paths and thresholds. Most funders have a threshold that turns a variance into a formal notice. When you're near it, every honest instinct you have will be tested by somebody who wants to stay just under it, and the forecast formula is where they'll try. The Code is plain. 5.3.1: we don't make misleading or false statements, state half truths, provide information out of context, or withhold information that would make our statements misleading or incomplete. The comment on 5.3.2 says half truths and non-disclosures intended to mislead stakeholders are as unprofessional as affirmatively making misrepresentations. And 2.3.1 asks us to uphold the policies and rules that govern our work, which includes the threshold you'd rather not cross.

The aspirational standard under 5.2.3 is accurate information in a timely manner, and its comment says we need the courage to share bad news even when it may be poorly received. I'd like that sentence to have been on the ninth floor in December 2034. I'm not sure it would have helped. I was the one who'd have had to read it.

When somebody asks you for one number, give them the most likely one, with its range and what drives it, and tell them when the next one will come. A single number with the uncertainty sanded off is the same lie as a single duration. You learned that on page three.
That's page five. Do the arithmetic before you open your mouth. Say the number you'd say if the person who'll pay for it was in the room. Somebody always is.

How the exam asks it. For oversight reporting, the best answer gives accurate indexes, a forecast range, causes, a recovery plan, and the decisions needed, and follows the reporting rules even when the news crosses a threshold.

Thursday, June 2. The man from finance had a ledger now. In March he'd carried his laptop in both hands, like a tray. Today he carried the ledger under his arm, like a man who'd stopped expecting to be thanked for it.

Halcyon's reserve ledger through May, in millions. The contingency reserve, inside the cost baseline: 96 at baseline, 38.6 drawn for the stack line, pump 2, the storm and JB-7, and 57.4 left. The management reserve, held by the ARA outside the baseline: 72, none of it drawn. And the valve work is open, with no funding source assigned.

The second test article work package the change board had approved in May, $7.2 million with its own contingency inside it, had no funding source code yet. Neither did the root cause work's $1.9 million: the life test instrumentation, Aldergrove's teardown support, and the analysis. Together, $9.1 million. Aldergrove would invoice at delivery, in July. None of it was spent. All of it was committed.

Garrett had sent a note that morning. Ask Calvin for management reserve. That's what it's for. Keep our contingency clean for the launch campaign. The man from finance had a different idea, and he said it the way a man says something he's said at other companies. Or Tallgrass carries it in overhead this year, and nobody's CPI moves.
Quinn had the board's minutes on the table, open to item four. She didn't say anything. She put one finger on the words cannot be absorbed, and left it there.
Garrett wants management reserve, and finance wants overhead. How should Sam fund the valve work?
Answer. Fund the valve work from the ARA's management reserve through Calvin's office.
B. Spread the valve work across the stage integration, test, and assembly control accounts.
C. Fund the valve work from Tallgrass overhead this year and keep it off the program's books.
D. Fund the valve work from program contingency and give it its own control account.

Sam signs the transfer at the table. The money moves out of the contingency line into a new control account called AR 2207 INVESTIGATION, which is what item four asked for, and the cost baseline doesn't change by a dollar, because contingency was already inside it. Quinn writes the new remaining balance on the ledger on the wall in red pen and dates it. The man from finance reads the new account name twice. The partners will see that line. That's why it's there. He thinks about it, and then, which surprises Sam, he nods. I've never had a board ask for that before. Sam sends Calvin's office the draw and the balance the same afternoon, one paragraph, and a note on how much of it is committed and how much is already spent, so nobody looks for all of it in June's actual cost.

That's a go. AR 2207 is in the risk register, so its responses are paid from contingency, which the project manager manages. Moving contingency into a work package leaves the baseline alone and changes the reserve balance, so you report the draw and what remains. Management reserve is for the unforeseen, and hiding a cost in overhead hides it from the people paying.

Monday, June 13. Wendell had been back from Albuquerque since May 20 with a sunburn on the back of his neck and opinions about Pump 2 that Paloma had asked him to write down. Arlo Dunn was back on nights at the stand, and when Wendell was on the console Arlo found reasons to be in the blockhouse.

The man from finance had found the biggest labor variance in the propulsion account, and it had a name. The resource plan priced the test conductor at Tallgrass's standard rate, forty hours a week. Wendell had retired in 2058 and come back the next spring as a contractor at a rate a third higher, and he'd worked nights, and he'd billed every hour, because he billed every hour. By June he'd already worked more than the plan gave him for the year.
And July and August belonged to the test article's life test, five weeks of cold cycles, every one of them with Wendell on the console.

Garrett had a solution, as usual. Put Arlo on the console. He's trained, he's half the rate, and Wendell can consult. The man from finance had another one. Or we book Wendell to the facility account. He's carried as a facilities contractor anyway. Propulsion goes back on plan.
Wendell wasn't in the room. He was at the stand. Arlo was, because he'd come in to pick up a cable, and he stood very still by the door and looked at the floor.
Wendell has already worked more hours than the plan gave him for the year. What should Sam do?
Answer. Charge Wendell's hours to the facility account, where he's carried as a contractor.
B. Put Arlo on the console for the summer firings and keep Wendell on call as a consultant.
C. Re-plan Wendell at his real rate, with Arlo paired beside him on every cycle.
D. Keep Wendell on the console but cap his hours at the plan's figure for the year.

Quinn rewrites the resource plan for propulsion that afternoon with Wendell's actual rate, the nights he really works, and a rule he agrees to on the phone: no more than five nights in seven, and never a night alone. Arlo goes on the plan by name, beside Wendell for every cycle, paid as what he is, the second person who'll be able to do this. The difference goes into the bottom up estimate for what's left, where it belongs. Sam calls Wendell and tells him what they did. There's a long pause on the line. You put my real number in the plan. It was always the real number, Sam says. The plan was wrong. Huh. Arlo, by the door, takes a notebook out of his pocket, a narrow one with a spiral at the top, and writes something in it.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Define and plan resources from what the work requires, at what they actually cost and when they're actually available. When the plan is wrong about a person, correct the plan and the estimate. Pairing a second person also reduces a single point of failure.

Friday, July 1. 7:00 AM. June had closed at midnight. Quinn had been in since five with the control account reports on one screen and the baseline on the other, and coffee she'd forgotten on the windowsill.

Every owner had sent a number. Hana's departure stage reported its qualification work ninety two percent complete, which was the share of its budget spent. The habitat team claimed half the value of every work package it had started. Rafa's report said the flight software was seventy percent done, because seventy percent of the planned sprints had happened.

If I add up what everybody sent, Quinn said, earned value is 1,262 million and CPI is 0.99, and we're the best run program in the agency. She put both hands flat on the table. If I use the earning rules we wrote into the plan in March, it isn't.

The plan's rules were on the wall where she'd taped them in March. Short hardware packages earned nothing until they were done. Long ones earned at weighted milestones, each one a thing you could walk out and look at. Software earned by story points accepted against the program's definition of done, out of the points in the release plan. Nobody had used them yet. This was the first month it mattered.
Quinn has two ways to add up earned value, and they don't agree. What goes in the report?
Answer. Report earned value by the earning rules for hardware and leave software out of it.
B. Report earned value by the earning rules in the plan for both hardware and software.
C. Report earned value from each owner's own percent complete and the sprint counts.
D. Report earned value as percent of budget spent, the one figure finance can audit.

It takes Quinn and two owners until three. The departure stage, measured by its milestones, has earned eighty one percent of its qualification value, not ninety two. The habitat team's half credit for started work comes out. Rafa's team, measured by accepted points, has earned sixty one percent of its release, which Rafa says is about what he'd have guessed if anyone had asked him instead of his sprint count. The totals go on one page.Halcyon, cumulative to June 30 2061, millions. Status date June 30. Earned value by the plan's earning rules: weighted milestones for hardware, accepted story points for software.Three bars. Planned, 1,250 million. Earned, 1,200. Spent, 1,280. They'd done less than they planned, and they'd paid more for it than it was worth. Rafa reads it and laughs once. Almost done earns nothing. I've been saying that to my people for six years. Nobody ever said it to me. Hana reads it and doesn't laugh, and then she asks Quinn for the milestone list for the rest of the year, so she'll know what she can earn.

Exactly right. Develop metrics and reconcile them: earned value comes from earning rules agreed before the work, applied the same way to everyone. Hybrid work needs both kinds: objective milestones for hardware and accepted story points for software. Then the indexes mean something.
Tuesday, July 5. Quinn had four estimates at completion on the whiteboard in a column, in four colors, with the formula above each one in black and the budget, 2,400 million, written across the top.

She walked Sam down the column with the cap of the marker. Budget over CPI. That one says we keep spending the way we have. 2,560. The next. Spent so far, plus the rest at budget. That one says the bad spring never happens again. 2,480. The third. Spent so far, plus the rest divided by CPI times SPI. That one says the overrun and the slip both keep going. 2,613. She tapped the fourth, which was blank. And the owners' own bottom up number. Due Friday.

Beside the column she'd written her variance analysis, because she said you couldn't pick a formula without one. Of the $80 million cost variance, $9 million was one time: the storm stand down and restart, Pump 2, JB-7. The other $71 million came from the stack line's yield and the Breather fabrication's rework, and both of those were still happening. Under that, in her capitals: THE WINDOW DOESN'T MOVE. EVERY DAY OF SPI WE'RE SHORT, WE BUY BACK.
Garrett was on the speaker from his car. Use the second one. The storm was one time. The pump was one time. That's the honest formula for a program that had a bad spring.
Quinn looked at Sam and didn't say anything. The second one was the lowest of the four.
Quinn has four estimates at completion, and Garrett wants the one time formula. Which forecast should Sam give?
Answer. Forecast 2,613 from the CPI times SPI formula with the bottom up check behind it.
B. Hold the forecast at the 2,400 BAC until the bottom up estimate arrives Friday.
C. Forecast 2,480 from AC plus BAC minus EV, treating the overrun as one time.
D. Forecast 2,560 from BAC divided by CPI, the standard formula for typical variance.

Sam writes the reasons beside the third number on the board: the overrun is mostly ongoing, the program is behind, and the window won't move, so both indexes will drive what's left. What's been spent, plus the work that's left at the efficiency both indexes together say it'll get, comes to 2,613. Then he tells Garrett, on the speaker, that the forecast will go out with that number and the bottom up estimate beside it, both explained. On Friday the control account owners' estimate comes in: 1,320 left to spend, an EAC of 2,600. Quinn holds the two numbers up side by side. Half a percent apart. From two directions. She circles both. That's the first time I've believed a forecast in this building. Garrett, on the speaker, says nothing for long enough that they both check the call is still connected.

That's a go. Choose the EAC formula from the cause. Here the cost variance is ongoing and the fixed window means the schedule shortfall will be bought back with money, so the CPI x SPI formula fits. A bottom up estimate checks it. Two methods that agree are worth more than one that's convenient.
Decision five. One point oh seven.

Wednesday, July 6. 4:30 PM. Hale called from the back of a car in Washington, where she'd gone a week early to count votes. Garrett was in Sam's office for it, on the couch, with his shoes off, which he did when he wanted to look relaxed.

Sam. I've read Quinn's forecast. I need to ask you one question, and I need you to hear why I'm asking. Can the program finish inside $2.4 billion? If you tell me yes, I don't have to send eleven governments a notice by the end of the month. If I send that notice, two of them will use it.
The team will find efficiencies, Garrett said. They always do. Tell her yes, and we'll manage to it.

Quinn had come to the door with a sheet of paper and stopped there. On the paper were two numbers, each one a to complete performance index, the TCPI. To finish inside the budget, every dollar left had to buy a dollar and seven cents of work. To finish at 2,600, it only had to buy ninety one cents. Under them was the program's CPI since March, month by month. It had never once been above 0.97.
Hale asks if the program can finish inside 2.4 billion dollars. How should Sam answer her?
Answer. Cut enough of the remaining test program to bring the forecast down to the BAC.
B. Tell Hale yes on 2.4 billion and give the teams a stretch target to get there.
C. Commit to 2.4 billion as a goal and show the 2.6 forecast beside it every month.
D. Tell Hale a TCPI of 1.07 isn't credible and bring her options to close the gap.

He reads her the two numbers and the history. To finish on 2.4, the rest of the program has to run about fourteen percent better than it has run so far. To finish on 2.6, it has to keep doing what it's doing. I can't tell you yes, ma'am. I can tell you what the choices are. He gives her three, from Quinn's sheet: fund the $200 million above the baseline, which keeps the $72 million of management reserve for the unknowns, or take scope out through the change board with the crew and the board consulted, or a mix. The car goes quiet. Then Hale says, Garrett. Imogen. Did you know the CPI had never been above 0.97? Garrett puts his shoes back on. Hale asks Sam to send her the sheet. She doesn't say what she'll do with it. She says she'd rather send a notice she believes than a yes she doesn't.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. TCPI shows the efficiency the remaining work would need. Compare it with the CPI to date: 1.07 against 0.94 isn't a credible target. Anticipate the finance challenge, say so plainly, and work with governance on real options. Never force the estimate to match the budget.

Thursday, July 7. The trajectory team's memo was two paragraphs long, and Quinn had read it nine times. The baseline burn was Sunday, February 18, 2063. The last departure date the trajectory team would sign was Sunday, March 4. After that the energy to reach Mars on a 200 day transfer climbed faster than the departure stage could pay for it.

Fourteen days. They weren't in the schedule. They'd never been in the schedule, because the schedule ended on February 18. They were just there, at the end of the window, the way the high bay had a mezzanine nobody used.

Everybody had found them at once. Garrett's investor deck, the June edition, said two weeks of margin inside the window on its fourth page. Gwen Talley, Hale's chief of staff, had called to ask whether the program could show February 4 again, now that there was room. Rafa wanted a week of it for the autonomy work, in writing, before anyone else got it.

Sam had the gas bill in his shirt pocket, the way he'd had it in March. On Ada's number the ship already arrived nine days after the reserve ran out. On the ARA's model there were fifty eight days to spare. Fourteen days fit on one of those numbers and not the other.
Fourteen days of margin just turned up, and everybody wants them. What should Sam do with them?
Answer. Split the fourteen days among the hardware, software, and crew paths as extra float.
B. Declare the fourteen days as schedule reserve and set rules for drawing it down.
C. Offer Hale the fourteen days to bring launch back to February 4, ahead of the vote.
D. Keep the fourteen days off every chart as a quiet reserve for real trouble.

Quinn adds a line to the schedule that has never been there: SCHEDULE RESERVE, 14 DAYS, FEB 18 TO MAR 4, 2063. Under it she writes the rules Sam asks for. Nobody plans work into it. A draw is requested at the change board, with the cause and the days, and every draw is reported to Hale, the partners, and the readiness board in the next status, along with what's left. And beside it, in a note on every report from now on, the line Sam writes himself: On the station's own margin estimate, each day drawn is a day the colony doesn't have. Garrett's office takes page four out of the investor deck by Friday, after Sam calls. Rafa reads the rules and asks for his week through the change board, properly, and gets two days of something better: a simulator slot nobody was using. Gwen says the Director will want to know why the reserve can't be a date. Sam says because it's a reserve.

Exactly right. Schedule reserve is time held for identified risks, and like cost contingency it belongs in the baseline, declared, with rules for drawing it and reporting what's left. Hidden reserve breeds hidden spending. Reserve promised away as an earlier date is no longer reserve. Say what each day costs.

Monday, July 11. Page five had come in Friday's mail, green ink, Golden postmark. He'd read it at the kitchen table with the butter knife still in his hand, then in the truck in the Tallgrass lot, then again at his desk. He knew the 0830 line now the way he knew the 0912 line on page three. I said call it 0.9. He had the page folded in his inside pocket with the notebook.

At ten, Gwen called. The Director would like the program rebaselined to the new estimate before Thursday. She'd like the partners to see a program on plan from July forward. The variances start at zero. It's cleaner.
Garrett had been copied. He came down the hall to say he loved it. New baseline, new year. Nobody in that ballroom wants to look at last spring.
It would be the first change to the baseline since it was approved in March. Quinn had kept every month of history since then, and every approved change, in a binder on the shelf by the door.
The change board hadn't met on it. Nobody had asked it to.
Hale's office wants the program rebaselined to the new estimate before Thursday. How should Sam handle it?
Answer. Send the rebaseline through the change board and carry the variance history with it.
B. Rebaseline to the June 30 actuals before Thursday, as the Director's office asks.
C. Have Hale approve the new baseline herself this week, as the change board can't meet.
D. Keep the March baseline for the rest of the year and report against it as funded.

Quinn writes the change request that afternoon. It proposes a new cost baseline at the forecast of $2,600 million, with the $72 million of management reserve still held over it, for a total budget of $2,672 million, and says it takes effect only if and when the partners fund it. It carries the variance history forward, month by month, on its own page, and it says so on the cover. The change board meets Wednesday by phone, from three time zones, and approves it for submission. Sam calls Gwen back. So the variances don't go away. They happened, ma'am, Sam says. If the partners fund the new number, the program gets measured against it from then on. Last spring stays on the page. A pause. She's going to ask why. Because in two years somebody's going to want to know how we got here, and it'll be her.

That's a go. Rebaseline through change control, for approved changes and approved funding, and keep the variance history. Communicate the status of the proposed change and update the documents when it's approved. A baseline is a measuring stick; it isn't an eraser.

Tuesday, July 12. 10:15 PM. The hotel near Union Station had a bar off the lobby with green lamps on the tables and a television with the sound off, showing a ball game nobody watched. Garrett had found Sam there and bought him a club soda without asking, which was the kind of thing Garrett remembered about people.

Thursday, Garrett said. Let me tell you how Thursday goes. You stand up, you say 2.6. That's eight percent over. Rule 4.2 says anything five percent or more goes to the partners in a written notice within thirty days. Eleven parliaments read the word overrun in August. Two of them have elections in the fall. You've just given two candidates a speech.

He turned his glass. Or. The storm was one time. The pump was one time. You use the one time formula, you call the CPI 0.95, which is how everybody rounds, and it's 2,480. Three percent. No notice. We fix it in the fall, quietly, and the ship flies. Nobody lied. Every number on that slide is a number you can defend.
The program's plan said it reported under the ARA's financial rules, whoever had signed what. Rule 4.2 was one of them.

ARA FINANCIAL RULES RULE 4.2 (EXTRACT). AN ESTIMATE AT COMPLETION FIVE PERCENT OR MORE ABOVE ITS APPROVED COST BASELINE SHALL BE NOTIFIED IN WRITING TO THE PARTNER FINANCE COMMITTEE WITHIN THIRTY DAYS OF THE STATUS DATE ON WHICH IT IS FIRST FORECAST, WITH ITS CAUSES AND THE PROGRAM'S PLAN.
Page five was in his inside pocket. He could feel the fold against his ribs.
Garrett is pressing Sam to use his numbers on Thursday. How should Sam answer him?
Answer. Agree to Garrett's numbers for Thursday and send the full analysis after the vote.
B. Call Hale tonight about the pressure and ask her to keep Garrett out of the review.
C. Tell Garrett no tonight and that the five percent notice goes in Thursday's deck.
D. Tell Garrett he'll sleep on it and check with Calvin in the morning on the rule.

No. Garrett waits for more, and Sam gives it to him, evenly. Seventy one of the eighty is still happening. The one time formula isn't true for us, and 0.9375 isn't 0.95. The forecast crosses five percent, so it's a notice. I'll give it Thursday with the causes, the plan, the options, and the reserve. I'd like you standing next to me when I do. Garrett smiles, the wide one, the one Sam reads like a gauge. You're going to cost me a partner. Maybe. Rounding would cost you all of them in a year, and the ship with them. Garrett finishes his drink. He doesn't say yes. He doesn't say he won't be there. Upstairs, Sam writes three lines in his notebook about the conversation, with the time, and goes to bed, and doesn't sleep.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Governance sets the reporting rules and thresholds, and you follow them, especially when they're inconvenient. Say no clearly, give the reason, and offer the honest path with a plan. Recording a pressure conversation is good practice. Code 2.3.1 and 5.3.1.
Decision nine. Two in the morning.

Thursday, July 14. 2:04 AM. He'd gone into the bathroom to wash his face at two and stayed, sitting on the edge of the tub with the laptop on his knees, because the bathroom was the only place in the room without a window, and every window had the dome of the Capitol in it, lit up white, like an exam.

Slide 6 was open. Indexes and forecast. Everything else in the deck was done. This was the one he'd left for last, which he knew was a thing people did with the slide that mattered, and he'd done it anyway.
At 1:40 a text had come from Garrett: Slide 6. Last chance. .95. Everybody rounds.

He'd taken page five out of his pocket and unfolded it and put it on the closed lid beside the sink, and the water from washing his face had curled the edge of it a little. 0830. I said call it 0.9. He said 0.9 and improving. I didn't say improving. I didn't say not.

0.9375 looked a great deal like 0.95 at two in the morning. That was the thing he hadn't expected. It wasn't a lie he was looking at. It was a number that was nearly the number, and a formula that was in every textbook, and a man he'd known nineteen years saying everybody did it, and a woman who'd lost three people saying she had too.

He thought about the jet in Arizona. He didn't, as a rule. The rule had held for nineteen years and had stopped holding in February. A form with a box on it. An indication that came and went. An hour he didn't have. He'd signed it because it was nearly fine.
It's two in the morning, and 0.9375 looks a lot like 0.95. What should Sam show?
Answer. Show CPI 0.95 with the one time EAC, as Garrett asked, with the method in a footnote.
B. Show the trend lines from May on and give the exact figures to anyone who asks.
C. Show CPI 0.94 and the EAC range, and state on the slide that it triggers the notice.
D. Show the real indexes and EAC range but leave the notice for Calvin to raise.

He types 0.94, and then, because it's what Quinn would do, 0.9375 under it in small type. SPI 0.96. EAC 2,600 to 2,613, two methods, half a percent apart. One line on why: the stack line and the Breather, still happening, and a window that doesn't move. One line on the notice: this forecast crosses Rule 4.2, and the written notice will be filed with the committee by July 30, with the plan. One line on the decisions he needs from them. He reads it back once. It's the least encouraging slide he's ever made, and it's the first one in his life with a dollar sign on it that he'd sign. At 2:40 he texts Garrett one line back: 0.94. Then he goes to bed, and sleeps three hours, which is two more than he expected.

Exactly right. Communicate status accurately and completely: the real indexes, the forecast range from the methods that fit, the causes, and what the forecast triggers under the governance rules. Put it where the decision makers will see it. Code 5.2.3: the courage to share bad news even when it may be poorly received.

Thursday, July 14. 10:40 AM. The ballroom was called the Potomac Room, and it had chandeliers and a carpet in a pattern of gold leaves that seemed to move if you looked at it too long. The eleven delegations sat at long tables in a horseshoe, each with its flag on a little stand and its advisers behind it. The chair, a delegate in half glasses who had been a national auditor for twenty years before she was a delegate, sat at the top of the horseshoe. Calvin Osterhout, the ARA's comptroller, sat at her right hand with a stack of tabbed binders. Hale sat in the first row of the gallery. Garrett sat beside Sam at the witness table, which Sam hadn't been sure he would.

Slide 6 had gone up at 10:20. 0.94. 2,600 to 2,613. The notice line. The ballroom had gone quiet in the particular way a room of auditors goes quiet, and Calvin had written something on his pad and underlined it twice.

Now Calvin leaned toward his microphone. He was sixty, gray, with a bow tie that had been in fashion when he was a boy, and he spoke slowly, like a man counting the words. Mr. Okafor. Item 14. The live stream of the departure burn and the arrival. What does it cost to finish, and would the partners notice if it went?

In the first row, Hale didn't move. The stream had been her request in March. She'd said then what forty million people watching did to a budget vote, and half the people in this room were the vote. On Sam's tablet, Quinn had already sent the line for the stream: the remaining cost to finish it, a rounding error on the gap.
Calvin asks about the stream, and whether the partners would miss it. What should Sam say?
Answer. Defend the stream as the Director's request and the partners' public audience.
B. Give Calvin the real cost to finish, then route any cut through the change board.
C. Offer to cut the stream on the spot, as the comptroller is the one asking.
D. Say the stream is the Director's decision and ask Hale to answer it from the floor.

He gives Calvin the number from Rafa's backlog, and then the other half. It's small against the gap. It's what the Director and two of the partners count on for public support, and it depends on a guidance requalification the crew wants anyway. Cutting it saves money and costs you something the money doesn't show. If the committee wants it considered, I'll take it to the change board this month, with the Director and the software lead, and you'll have the decision and the reasons in writing. Calvin looks at him over the bow tie for a moment. That's the first answer this morning that didn't try to sell me anything. He makes a note. In the first row Hale lets out a breath Sam can see from the witness table.

That's a go. Osterhout wants every dollar to earn its keep. Hale and two partners want the audience. They're both your customers, so they both get the cost and the value from you, and the cut, if it comes, goes through the change board with the person who asked for the stream sitting at the table. Then you tell them when they'll hear.
Thursday, July 14. 11:35 AM. The chair took her half glasses off and folded them, which, Calvin had warned Sam in the hallway, meant she was about to ask the question she'd come for.
Mr. Okafor. Tonight I write a report to my finance minister. It has a box in it. The box holds one number. What do I write in it?
Slide 6 was still on the screen behind him: 2,600 to 2,613, and the notice line under it.

Garrett, beside him, had his pen down. In the gallery somebody's chair creaked. On Sam's tablet, Quinn, who was watching the session's feed in Watkins with the whole big room behind her, had sent one word: Range.
The chair's report has a box that holds one number. What should Sam tell her to write?
Answer. Give 2.48 billion, the lowest of the forecasts, the one she'll repeat to her minister.
B. Offer to send the full model after the session in place of a single number.
C. Give 2.613 billion, the formula's exact figure, as the one precise number for the box.
D. Give 2.6 billion as the most likely cost, with its range of 2.60 to 2.61 beside it.

Write 2.6 billion, ma'am. That's our most likely cost. Two methods put it between 2.60 and 2.61. What moves it is the stack line and the Breather fabrication, and whether we hold the date, and we'll have a new estimate at every quarterly review, the next one in October. If it moves by more than the rule says, you'll get a notice. The chair writes it down. Then she puts her glasses back on. Thank you. That's the number I'll write, and that's the date I'll look for the next one. Calvin, at her right, closes a binder.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. When a decision maker needs one number, give the most likely value, its range, its drivers, and when it will next be updated. That's a status they can act on and repeat accurately. A bare number with no range is false precision; a refusal is no help at all.

Thursday, July 14. 9:00 PM. The hotel desk faced a window with the dome in it, and he turned the chair so the dome was behind the tablet and out of the shot. One way light time tonight was nine minutes and thirty eight seconds. She'd get it before she slept, and watch it twice.

The committee would decide the funding in August. The notice would go out by July 30. Calvin had stopped him in the hallway after the session and said, I'll fight you on the money, Mr. Okafor. I won't have to fight you on the numbers. That's rarer than you'd think.

He was more tired than he'd been since the night of the storm. He'd been at a witness table for two hours and twenty minutes and his back said so. He had the notebook on the desk beside the tablet, open, and the hotel pen, and he hadn't written anything in it since Tuesday night.
He thought about the logs he'd sent her since February, and which ones he'd watched back before he sent them.
He pressed record. The red light came on.
Sam is recording for Ada after the review. What should his message say?
Answer. Tell her the money's short, he said so in the room, and the vote comes in August.
B. Tell her the review went fine and he'll explain the details after the vote.
C. Send her Quinn's forecast pack and the slides to read every number for herself.
D. Keep it light: the review went well, the partners are behind it, and money's fine.

He tells her plainly. The ship costs more than the budget, and the partners will decide in August whether to pay it or take something out. Nothing he said today changes the date. He tells her about the bow tie, because she'll want the bow tie, and about the carpet that moves if you look at it, and about the chair who wanted one number. He says he's tired. He says he was scared at two in the morning, and tells her why, in two sentences: slide 6, and the number he put on it. He doesn't do the voice. He watches it back once and sends it, and nine minutes and thirty eight seconds later it's on Mars.

Exactly right. Promote transparency with the stakeholders who depend on the outcome: what happened, what it means, what's decided next, and when. Plain, specific, and timely, without passing her confidential committee papers. The same honesty you owed the partners, at the scale of one person.

Friday, July 15. 7:40 AM in Washington, which was 5:40 at home. The tablet on the hotel desk made the two note chime, and he was awake for it, because he'd been awake since five, sitting in the chair by the window with the dome going from white to gray to stone as the sun came up behind it.
One way light time when she recorded it, nine minutes and thirty eight seconds. The first line, he'd learn, said she'd recorded it before she opened his.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3699. One way, 9 minutes 38 seconds. Margin, 774 days. Hi, Dad. I'm recording this before I open your log, because I wanted to say it before I hear what you say. There's one in the queue from you. I can see it sitting there. I'm not opening it yet. Don't be weird about that. Mom's watch says 11:40. So it's still her birthday for twenty minutes, at home. On ours it's been her birthday all sol, because I decided it was. I planted peppers for her. In Bay D, in the corner by the air handler where it's warmest. Not the scotch bonnets, we don't have those, nobody brought them, I asked. A jalapeño line somebody's grandmother smuggled up in fifty six in a sock, which Pilar swears is a true story. Six seeds. I'll tell you if they come up. Mom would say jalapeños don't count. Mom would plant them anyway. Is the pot still on the back step? The clay one. You don't have to tell me. I'm only asking. Hollis read the ARA's summary of your budget review at dinner. It said an estimate of 2.6 billion and a notice to the partners. Then he said the partners were fully committed to the schedule, and he said committed four times, and everybody clapped, and I didn't, and Teodor didn't, and Pilar was in Bay D with the peppers. Stack four quit again four weeks ago. I told you. So, 774. Same minus nine. That doesn't change because a room in Washington had a meeting. One more thing. And then I'll open yours. Your budget face is in the frame, Dad. It has been for three logs. Your eyes go up and to the left, like there's a spreadsheet on the ceiling, and you do it right after you say something's fine. You did it the year Mom's insurance stopped paying. You did it for a whole year. I was thirteen, and I knew what it meant then, and I know now. I don't know what you're rounding. I know you are. I'd rather have the number. Okay. Opening yours now. Love you. 774. Ada out.
He watched it twice. The second time he paused it where she said the pot, and sat there.

Then he picked up his phone, because he knew before he looked, the way he'd known about the date on AR 2207 before he checked it. The reminder was still in the list, the one he'd set eleven years ago and never changed. One letter. G. It had come up at 6:00 AM on Thursday, while he was in the shower he hadn't taken at two and had taken at six, and he'd swiped it away without reading it, on his way to slide 6, the way you swipe away a thing that's always there.

July 14. He'd written it at the top of every page of the deck. He'd written it on the whiteboard behind his desk in June, under WASHINGTON. He'd said it out loud in the ballroom, into a microphone, twice.

The clay pot was on the back step in Aurora. It had been there since before Ada could walk. Grace had grown scotch bonnets in it every summer until the summer she got sick, too hot for anybody but her, and he'd never emptied it, and every spring something came up in it on its own, grass mostly, and once, the year Ada turned sixteen, one pepper plant nobody had planted, which neither of them had ever talked about.

She'd opened his log hours ago, right after she said so. The one where he'd told her the money was short, and that he'd said so in the room, and what the partners would decide, and about slide 6 at two in the morning. She'd asked for the number. She had it now, and she'd recorded this one not knowing what was in it.

On the program's charts, since July 7, there were fourteen days at the end of the window with a line of his own under them. Each day drawn is a day the colony doesn't have. He'd written it about a number he took from her. He hadn't thought until now that she'd see it someday, on some feed, and know where he'd got it.

Seven weeks of arithmetic. Most of it, he thought, he'd done in the right order this time, and he didn't like thinking it, because in his experience that thought turned up about a day before the phone rang.

The laptop was on the desk to the right of the tablet. That was where it had sat on the kitchen table at home, every night in June, with Quinn's spreadsheet open on it, tipped away from the lens so the camera wouldn't catch it, which he'd taken to mean it wasn't in the log. He sat back down. Camera first, the black dot over the screen. Laptop. Then his eyes went where Ada said they went, up and to the left, before he could stop them. There was a sprinkler head up there, and a water stain about the shape of Kansas, and no spreadsheet, and there never had been.
So it hadn't been out of the frame. She'd been watching him read it off the ceiling.

He pressed record. Happy birthday to your mother, he said. His voice did something on mother, and he let it. I forgot, Ada. I wrote the date on every page of a slide deck and I forgot. I'm sorry. I'll go out Saturday and look in the pot, and I'll tell you what's in it, even if it's grass. It's usually grass.

Then he told her the number. Point nine three seven five. Two point six billion dollars. A letter to eleven governments by the thirtieth, his name on it. He looked straight at the dot for all of it and his neck ached by the end, like after a ramp inspection in Tucson in August. He didn't watch it back. Kansas stayed put.
